prompt: How far forward should you sit on the motorcycle?
choices: Far enough back that your arms are fully straight
As far forward as possible, with chest over the tank
Wherever your feet can rest flat on the ground
Far enough forward that your arms are slightly bent
explanation: Sit far enough forward so your arms are slightly bent when you hold the handgrips. Bent arms let you press on the handlebars without reaching too far.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 11 (Body Position)

prompt: How should you hold the handgrips at the start of a ride?
choices: Loosely, with your right wrist bent upward
With only your fingertips, wrist dropped low
Firmly, with your right wrist flat
Firmly, with your right wrist rolled down
explanation: Hold the handgrips firmly to keep your grip over rough surfaces. Starting with your right wrist flat helps keep you from accidentally using too much throttle.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 11 (Body Position)

prompt: What is the main reason to start with your right wrist flat on the throttle grip?
choices: It lets you reach the clutch lever more quickly
It helps prevent accidentally using too much throttle
It keeps the front brake lever from being squeezed
It lowers your hand below the mirror for a better view
explanation: A flat right wrist helps keep you from accidentally rolling on too much throttle, for example when you hit a bump.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 11 (Body Position)

prompt: Where should your hands be in relation to your elbows?
choices: Even with or below your elbows
Well above the level of your elbows
Even with your shoulders
Higher than your chin
explanation: Adjust the handlebars so your hands are even with or below your elbows. This lets you use the proper muscles for steering.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 11 (Body Position)

prompt: Why should you keep your knees against the gas tank?
choices: To keep your legs warm from engine heat in cold weather
To reduce wind drag at highway speeds
To keep your feet from reaching the shift lever by accident
To help you keep your balance as the motorcycle turns
explanation: Keeping your knees against the gas tank helps you keep your balance as the motorcycle turns.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 11 (Body Position)

prompt: Where should your feet be while riding?
choices: Firmly on the footrests, near the controls
Hovering just above the road for balance
Resting on the engine guards, away from the controls
On the footrests, with toes pointed down
explanation: Keep your feet firmly on the footrests to maintain balance, and near the controls so you can reach them easily. Don't drag your feet.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 11 (Body Position)

prompt: Why shouldn't you let your toes point downward while riding?
choices: It makes it impossible to reach the rear brake
It puts too much weight on the front wheel
They can catch between the road and the footrests
It causes the side stand to drop down
explanation: Don't let your toes point downward, because they may get caught between the road and the footrests.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 11 (Body Position)

prompt: Where is the gearshift lever on most motorcycles, and how is it operated?
choices: In front of the right footrest, with the right foot
In front of the left footrest, with the left foot
On the left handgrip, with the left thumb
Behind the left footrest, with the left heel
explanation: The gearshift lever is in front of the left footrest and is operated by the left foot. The right foot operates the rear brake.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 11 (Shifting Gears)

prompt: How do you shift to a higher gear on a typical motorcycle?
choices: Press the shift lever down with your toe and release
Hold the shift lever up until the engine speed drops off
Push the shift lever forward with your heel
Put your foot under the lever, then lift and release
explanation: To shift up, position your foot under the shift lever, lift and release. To downshift, press the lever down and release.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 11 (Shifting Gears)

prompt: On a typical motorcycle with a 1-N-2-3-4-5 pattern, how is neutral selected?
choices: Half lift from 1st, or half press from 2nd
A full press down from 1st gear with the clutch out
A full lift from 2nd gear while holding the brake
A quick double press down from 1st gear
explanation: Neutral sits between 1st and 2nd. It is selected by a half lift from 1st or a half press from 2nd.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 11 (Shifting Gears)

prompt: When should you shift up to a higher gear?
choices: Only when the engine reaches its maximum recommended RPM
Before the engine over-revs, but not so soon that it lugs
As early as possible, even if the engine lugs
Only after the engine starts to sound strained at high RPM
explanation: Shift up well before the engine reaches its maximum recommended RPM, but not so soon that the engine lugs.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 12 (Shifting Gears)

prompt: What is the first step of the MSF's 3-step upshift?
choices: Lift the shift lever firmly as far as it will go
Ease out the clutch lever and roll on the throttle
Roll off the throttle as you squeeze the clutch lever
Apply the rear brake while lifting the shift lever
explanation: Upshift: 1) roll off the throttle as you squeeze the clutch, 2) lift the shift lever firmly and release, 3) smoothly ease out the clutch and adjust the throttle.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 12 (Shifting Gears)

prompt: Besides slowing or stopping, when else does the manual say you may downshift?
choices: When you want to save fuel on the highway
Whenever you are in the middle of a sharp turn
Only when climbing a steep hill
When you need more power to accelerate
explanation: You should shift down through the gears as you slow or stop, and you can also shift down when you need more power to accelerate.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 12 (Shifting Gears)

prompt: What can happen if you shift into a lower gear while riding too fast for that gear?
choices: The front wheel will lift off the ground
It may lurch, and the rear wheel may skid
The engine will shut off to protect itself
The transmission will refuse to shift
explanation: Make certain you are riding slowly enough before shifting into a lower gear. If not, the motorcycle will lurch, and the rear wheel may skid.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 12 (Shifting Gears)

prompt: You are riding down a long hill and need to downshift. What may be necessary first?
choices: Use the brakes to slow enough to downshift safely
Shift into neutral and coast down the hill
Speed up so the engine can absorb the downshift
Downshift two gears at once without using the clutch
explanation: When riding downhill or shifting into first gear, you may need to use the brakes to slow sufficiently before downshifting safely.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 12 (Shifting Gears)

prompt: During a downshift, why roll on the throttle slightly as you ease out the clutch?
choices: It keeps the rear brake from locking during the shift
It is needed to move the shift lever back to center
It helps the engine come up to speed more quickly
It cancels the engine braking effect completely
explanation: Rolling on the throttle slightly while smoothly easing out the clutch helps the engine come up to speed more quickly and makes the downshift smoother.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 12 (Shifting Gears)

prompt: What is "engine braking"?
choices: Using the engine cut-off switch to slow down
Pressing the rear brake while holding in the clutch
The slowing effect of shifting to a lower gear
Turning off the engine while coasting in neutral
explanation: Shifting to a lower gear causes an effect similar to using the brakes. This is known as engine braking.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 12 (Shifting Gears)

prompt: How should you use engine braking smoothly?
choices: Downshift one gear at a time, easing out the clutch between shifts
Squeeze the clutch, drop straight into first gear and release quickly
Downshift several gears at once and let the clutch out quickly
Shift into neutral between each gear so the engine can cool
explanation: Shift down one gear at a time and ease out the clutch through the friction zone between each downshift, staying there until engine speed stabilizes.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 12 (Shifting Gears)

prompt: While you are stopped at a light, which gear should you be in?
choices: Neutral, with the clutch fully released
Second gear, for a smoother start
Neutral, with the engine cut-off switch off
First gear, so you can move out quickly
explanation: Remain in first gear while you are stopped so that you can move out quickly if you need to, such as to avoid a vehicle approaching from behind.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 12 (Shifting Gears)

prompt: When is it best to change gears for a turn?
choices: In the middle of the turn
Before entering the turn
At the sharpest point of the turn
Only after leaving the turn
explanation: It is best to change gears before entering a turn. If you must shift in the turn, do it smoothly, because a sudden change in power to the rear wheel can cause a skid.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 12 (Shifting Gears)

prompt: You realize you must shift while already in a curve. What is the main risk, and how should you shift?
choices: The front brake may lock, so squeeze it while shifting
The engine may stall, so shift quickly and release the clutch fast
There is no added risk, so shift the same way you would on a straight
A sudden power change can make the rear wheel skid, so shift smoothly
explanation: Sometimes shifting in a turn is necessary. Do it smoothly, because a sudden change in power to the rear wheel can cause a skid.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 12 (Shifting Gears)

prompt: When should you use both the front and rear brakes?
choices: Only in emergency stops
Only above about 30 mph
Every time you slow or stop
Only on dry, clean pavement
explanation: Always use both brakes every time you slow or stop. Using both for normal stops builds the skill you need in an emergency.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 12 (Braking)

prompt: The front brake can provide how much of a motorcycle's total stopping power?
choices: 70% or more
About 25%
About 50%
Less than the rear brake
explanation: The front brake is more powerful and can provide 70% or more of your total stopping power. It is safe to use if you use it properly.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 12 (Braking)

prompt: A new rider avoids the front brake because they believe it will throw them over the handlebars. What does the manual say?
choices: They are right; the rear brake should do most of the work
Used properly, it is safe and supplies most stopping power
The front brake is only safe at very low speeds, such as in parking lots
The front brake should be used only in emergencies
explanation: The front brake can provide 70% or more of your stopping power and is safe to use properly: squeeze it smoothly and progressively, without grabbing.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 12 (Braking)

prompt: During a hard straight-line stop, where should your knees and eyes be?
choices: Knees away from the tank, eyes on the front wheel
Knees against the tank, eyes on the road just ahead of the tire
Knees spread wide for balance, eyes on your mirrors
Knees against the tank, eyes up and looking well ahead
explanation: Keep your knees against the tank and your eyes up, looking well ahead. This helps you stop the motorcycle in a straight line; looking down at the road just ahead makes that harder.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 13 (Braking)

prompt: How should you apply the front brake?
choices: Grab it quickly with full force so you stop as fast as possible
Squeeze it smoothly and firmly, with progressively more force
Pump it rapidly on and off with light pressure
Apply it only after the rear wheel starts to slow
explanation: Squeeze the front brake smoothly, firmly and with progressively more force. Do not grab the lever or use abrupt pressure.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 13 (Braking)

prompt: As you brake hard in a straight line, the motorcycle's weight shifts forward. How does this affect the brakes?
choices: The rear gains traction, so you should press harder on the pedal
Each wheel loses traction equally, so ease off both brakes
Front traction increases and rear traction decreases
Weight transfer does not change traction at either wheel
explanation: As weight transfers forward, more traction is available at the front, so the front brake can be applied more firmly. Less traction is available at the rear, so use light-to-lighter rear pressure.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 13 (Braking)

prompt: During a hard straight-line stop, how should you apply the rear brake?
choices: With light-to-lighter pressure to avoid a rear-wheel skid
With steadily increasing pressure until the wheel locks
As hard as possible, since it does most of the stopping
Not at all; only the front brake should be used in hard stops
explanation: Apply light-to-lighter pressure to the rear brake pedal to prevent a rear wheel skid, because less traction is available at the rear as weight shifts forward.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 13 (Braking)

prompt: Why does the manual recommend using both brakes even for normal stops?
choices: It wears both brake pads evenly so they last longer
It builds the skill you need for emergency stops
It keeps the brake light from staying on too long
It is the only way to turn on the brake light
explanation: Using both brakes for even normal stops lets you develop the proper skill of using both brakes in an emergency.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 13 (Braking)

prompt: You need to stop while leaned over in a curve, and road and traffic conditions allow it. What is the best technique?
choices: Brake as hard as possible while keeping the same lean
Use only the rear brake and keep leaning
Lean further into the curve and apply the front brake hard
Bring the motorcycle as upright as possible, then brake
explanation: Any lean reduces traction available for braking. To stop as quickly and safely as possible in a curve, try to get the motorcycle as perpendicular to the road as possible, then brake.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 13 (Braking in a Corner)

prompt: If you must brake while still leaned over in a curve, how should you do it?
choices: Brake with full force, the same as you would when upright
Grab the front brake to slow quickly before the lean increases
Smoothly and gradually, with less force than when upright
Avoid braking at all until you leave the curve
explanation: If conditions don't allow straightening first, brake smoothly and gradually with less force than when upright. As you slow and reduce lean, you can brake more firmly.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 13 (Braking in a Corner)

prompt: On a motorcycle with a linked braking system, what happens when you use only the rear brake pedal?
choices: Braking pressure is applied to both the front and rear brakes
Only the rear brake is applied, as on any motorcycle
The anti-lock system turns off until you use the front lever
The engine cut-off switch is activated to slow the motorcycle
explanation: Linked braking connects the front and rear brakes and applies pressure to both when either the lever or the pedal is used. Check the owner's manual for how your system works.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 13 (Linked and Integrated Braking Systems)

prompt: What is an anti-lock braking system (ABS) designed to do?
choices: Prevent wheel lock-up and skids in panic stops
Make the motorcycle stop in half the normal distance
Apply the brakes automatically when an object is detected
Allow you to brake hard while leaned over at any speed
explanation: ABS prevents wheel lock-up and helps avoid skids in panic stops. When sensors detect a possible lock, it releases and reapplies brake pressure, more than 15 times per second.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 13 (Anti-Lock Braking Systems (ABS))

prompt: What are the four steps the MSF manual uses to describe turning?
choices: Look, lean, brake, accelerate
Signal, brake, steer, shift
Slow, look, press, roll
Slow, shift, lean, brake
explanation: Turning: SLOW before the turn, LOOK through it, PRESS the handgrip in the direction of the turn, and ROLL on the throttle.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 14 (Turning)

prompt: In the SLOW step of turning, how should you reduce speed?
choices: Apply the front brake hard once you are leaned in the turn
Shift into neutral and coast through the turn
Wait until you are in the turn, then use the rear brake
Close the throttle and, if needed, use both brakes
explanation: Reduce speed before the turn by closing the throttle and, if necessary, applying both brakes.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 14 (Turning)

prompt: How should you look through a turn?
choices: Turn your head and shoulders together toward the exit
Turn just your head, not your shoulders; keep eyes level
Keep your eyes on the road just in front of the front tire
Tilt your head with the motorcycle as it leans
explanation: Look through the turn to where you want to go. Turn just your head, not your shoulders, and keep your eyes level with the horizon.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 14 (Turning)

prompt: To begin a left turn at normal speed, which handgrip do you press?
choices: The right handgrip
Equal pressure on each handgrip
The left handgrip
No handgrip; you lean your body only
explanation: To turn, the motorcycle must lean. Press the handgrip in the direction of the turn: press left, lean left, go left.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 14 (Turning)

prompt: Why must you press on a handgrip to start a turn at normal riding speeds?
choices: It applies a little front brake to slow you for the turn
The motorcycle must lean to turn; pressing starts the lean
It keeps the front wheel pointed straight through the turn
It moves your weight back so the rear tire grips better
explanation: To turn, the motorcycle must lean. Pressing the handgrip in the direction of the turn (countersteering) starts the lean: press right, lean right, go right.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 14 (Turning)

prompt: How does the needed lean angle change with speed and sharpness of a turn?
choices: Higher speed needs less lean angle
Sharper turns need less lean angle
Lean angle stays about the same at any speed
More speed or a sharper turn needs more lean
explanation: The higher the speed in a turn, or the sharper the turn, the greater the lean angle needs to be.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 14 (Turning)

prompt: What should you do with the throttle in the ROLL step of a turn?
choices: Roll it on to maintain or slightly increase speed
Close it completely and coast through the turn
Roll it on hard to accelerate out quickly
Hold the clutch in while keeping the throttle closed
explanation: Roll on the throttle to maintain or slightly increase speed through the turn. This helps stabilize the motorcycle.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 14 (Turning)

prompt: In a normal turn, how should the rider's body lean compared with the motorcycle?
choices: The rider stays upright while only the motorcycle leans
The rider leans farther into the turn than the motorcycle
The rider leans the opposite way from the motorcycle
The rider and motorcycle lean together at the same angle
explanation: In regular turns, the rider and the motorcycle should lean together at the same angle. Keeping your body upright is for slow, tight turns.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 14 (Turning)

prompt: You are making a slow, tight U-turn in a parking lot. How should you position your body?
choices: Lean your body and the motorcycle together at the same angle
Keep your body upright and lean only the motorcycle
Lean your body farther into the turn than the motorcycle
Put both feet down and walk the motorcycle around
explanation: In slow, tight turns, counterbalance by leaning the motorcycle only and keeping your body upright. In normal turns, rider and motorcycle lean together.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 14 (Turning)

prompt: Why do riders often run into trouble in curves?
choices: They take curves too fast and can't hold the turn
They enter too slowly and lose their balance
They apply both brakes before reaching the curve
They look too far ahead instead of at the road surface
explanation: Riders often try to take curves too fast. When they can't hold the turn, they cross into another lane or go off the road, or they overreact and brake too hard, causing a skid.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 13 (Turning)

prompt: Why can a two-wheel motorcycle countersteer while a conventional three-wheel motorcycle cannot?
choices: Three-wheelers have no front brake to help with steering
Two-wheelers have wider handlebars than three-wheelers
A two-wheeler leans to turn; a three-wheeler cannot lean
Three-wheelers are too heavy for handgrip pressure to work
explanation: A two-wheel motorcycle must lean to turn, and pressing the handgrip starts the lean. Conventional three-wheel motorcycles cannot lean, so they cannot countersteer; the front wheel is pointed where the rider wants to go.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 49 (Three-Wheel Supplement: Steering & Tip)

prompt: On a motorcycle with an integrated braking system, what happens when you press the rear brake pedal?
choices: Only the rear brake is applied
Some front braking is applied as well
The front brake is fully applied instead
The anti-lock system is switched off
explanation: An integrated braking system is a variation of linked braking in which partial front braking is applied whenever the rear brake is activated. Check the owner's manual for how your system works.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 13 (Linked and Integrated Braking Systems)
